## Visualization, Debugging, and Data Manipulation

### Session 3

Today we will connect three skills:

``` text
visualize data
      ↓
recognize and solve problems
      ↓
manipulate data with dplyr
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Today is mostly practice

We will not cover every detail from Modules 5, 6, and 7.

The website contains the full explanations.

Today we will focus on the most important tools you need to keep working with your own data.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Load the data

Open your `intro-r-course` project.

Create a script called:

``` text
session-03.R
```

inside the `scripts/` folder.

Then run:

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| 
library(tidyverse)

recordTable <- read_csv(here::here("data", "recordTable.csv"))
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
library(tidyverse)

recordTable <- read_csv(
  "data/recordTable.csv"
)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Always inspect first

Before plotting or manipulating data:

``` r
head(recordTable)

dim(recordTable)

names(recordTable)

str(recordTable)
```

Ask:

- What does one row represent?
- What are the variables?
- Which columns are numeric?
- Which columns are categorical?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The logic of ggplot2

Most plots follow the same structure:

![](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/articles/ggplot2_files/figure-html/overview_graphic-1.png){fig-align="center"}

In R:

``` r
ggplot(
  data = my_data,
  aes(x = variable)
) +
  geom_something()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

There are many more options depending on what you want to explore or communicate with your data. If you want to go further, I recommend visiting these two websites: [R Charts](https://r-charts.com/distribution/) & [R Graph Gallery](https://r-graph-gallery.com/) \| ![](https://gpandradep.github.io/R-CameraTrap-Workshop/images/module-05/datavizexample.png){fig-align="center"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Make it readable

::::: columns
::: {.column width="30%"}
``` r

  data = recordTable,
  aes(x = Species)

```
:::

## Histograms

``` r
  theme_bw()
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Zooming without changing the data

``` r
ggplot(
  data = recordTable,
  aes(x = n_images)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 1,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(1, 20)
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

`coord_cartesian()` changes what we display, not the original data.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| 
ggplot(
  data = recordTable,
  aes(x = n_images)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 1,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(1, 20)
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Mapping vs. setting

Setting:

``` r
geom_point(color = "steelblue")
```

Every point has the same color.

Mapping:

``` r
geom_point(
  aes(color = Species)
)
```

Color represents a variable.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Common aesthetics

We can map or set:

``` text
color
fill
shape
size
alpha
```

Example:

``` r
ggplot(
  recordTable,
  aes(
    x = N_individuals,
    y = n_images,
    color = Species
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4)
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
ggplot(
  recordTable,
  aes(
    x = N_individuals,
    y = n_images,
    color = Species
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Focus on a few species

Sometimes a plot is easier to read if we focus on fewer groups.

```{r}
#| echo: true
common_species <- c(
  "White-tailed deer",
  "Armadillo",
  "Racoon",
  "Hog",
  "Virginia opossum"
)

common_records <- recordTable[
  recordTable$Species %in% common_species,
]
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Scatterplots

Question:

> Are records with more individuals associated with more images?

``` r
ggplot(
  data = common_records,
  aes(
    x = N_individuals,
    y = n_images,
    color = Species
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.4,
    size = 2
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
ggplot(
  data = common_records,
  aes(
    x = N_individuals,
    y = n_images,
    color = Species
  )
) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.4,
    size = 2
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## From raw records to summaries

Sometimes we need to summarize before plotting.

For example:

```{r}
#| echo: true
sp_counts <- recordTable |>
  count(
    Station,
    Species
  ) |>
  filter(
    Species %in% common_species
  )
sp_counts
```

Now each row represents:

``` text
one station × one species
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Boxplots

``` r
ggplot(
  data = sp_counts,
  aes(
    x = Species,
    y = n,
    fill = Species
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
ggplot(
  data = sp_counts,
  aes(
    x = Species,
    y = n,
    fill = Species
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw()
```

Here, the data are still counts.

Only the axis is displayed on a log scale.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Combining geometries

``` r
#| eval: true
ggplot(
  data = sp_counts,
  aes(
    x = Species,
    y = n,
    fill = Species
  )
) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw()
```

Each `+` adds a new layer.

```{r}

ggplot(
  data = sp_counts,
  aes(
    x = Species,
    y = n,
    fill = Species
  )
) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Which plot should I use?

| Variables             | Possible plot          |
|-----------------------|------------------------|
| one categorical       | bar plot               |
| one numeric           | histogram              |
| two numeric           | scatterplot            |
| categorical + numeric | boxplot or violin plot |

Start with the question:

> What do I want to show?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Saving plots

``` r
species_plot <- ggplot(
  recordTable,
  aes(x = Species)
) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw()

ggsave(
  filename = "outputs/species_records.png",
  plot = species_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 6,
  dpi = 300
)
```

## Data manipulation

Now we move from:

*plotting raw data*

to:

*preparing data for questions*

We will use `dplyr`.

Many `dplyr` functions are verbs.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Important dplyr verbs

| Function      | Action              |
|---------------|---------------------|
| `select()`    | choose columns      |
| `filter()`    | choose rows         |
| `arrange()`   | sort rows           |
| `rename()`    | rename columns      |
| `mutate()`    | create columns      |
| `count()`     | count observations  |
| `group_by()`  | create groups       |
| `summarise()` | calculate summaries |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Select columns

`select()` works with columns.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| 
selected_records <- recordTable |>
  select(
    Station,
    Species,
    N_individuals,
    Age,
    n_images
  )

selected_records
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Filter rows

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

deer_records <- recordTable |>
  filter(
    Species == "White-tailed deer"
  )

deer_records
```

`filter()` works with rows.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Multiple conditions

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

recordTable |>
  filter(
    Species == "White-tailed deer",
    N_individuals > 1
  )
```

Both conditions must be true.

This is like using:

*AND*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Several categories

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
recordTable |>
  filter(
    Species %in% c(
      "White-tailed deer",
      "Armadillo",
      "Racoon"
    )
  )
```

`%in%` asks:

> Is this value inside this group of possible values?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Rename columns

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| 
record_data <- recordTable |>
  rename(
    station = Station,
    species = Species,
    individuals = N_individuals,
    age = Age,
    images = n_images,
    date = Date,
    time = Time
  )
record_data
```

Now the column names are easier to type.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Create new columns

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
record_data <- record_data |>
  mutate(
    multiple_individuals = individuals > 1
  )

record_data
```

The new column is logical:

``` text
TRUE / FALSE
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Count records

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
record_data |>
  count(
    species,
    sort = TRUE
  )
```

The result has one row per species.

The column `n` contains the number of records.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Count combinations

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
record_data |>
  count(
    station,
    species
  )
```

Now each row represents:

``` text
one station × one species
```

This is a different unit than the original data.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Group and summarize

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
species_summary <- record_data |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    stations = n_distinct(station),
    total_individuals = sum(
      individuals,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
species_summary 
```

Now each row represents one species.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Always ask

``` text
What does one row represent?
```

Before summarizing:

``` text
1 row = 1 camera-trap record
```

After summarizing by species:

``` text
1 row = 1 species
```

After summarizing by station:

``` text
1 row = 1 station
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Pipes

The pipe:

``` r
|>
```

passes the result of one step into the next step.

Read it as:

``` text
then
```

Example:

``` r
recordTable |>
  filter(Species == "White-tailed deer") |>
  count(Station)
```

![](https://gpandradep.github.io/R-CameraTrap-Workshop/images/module-07/Pipe.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## A complete pipeline

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| 
common_species <- c(
  "White-tailed deer",
  "Armadillo",
  "Racoon",
  "Hog",
  "Virginia opossum"
)

common_summary <- recordTable |>
  filter(
    Species %in% common_species
  ) |>
  group_by(Species) |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    stations = n_distinct(Station),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(
    desc(records)
  )

common_summary 
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summaries can become plots

``` r
ggplot(
  common_summary,
  aes(
    x = Species,
    y = records,
    fill = Species
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#| eval: true
ggplot(
  common_summary,
  aes(
    x = Species,
    y = records,
    fill = Species
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw()
```

Use `geom_col()` when the counts already exist in the data.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Session workflow

``` text
import data
      ↓
inspect
      ↓
visualize
      ↓
debug when needed
      ↓
select / filter
      ↓
group / summarize
      ↓
visualize summaries
      ↓
export results
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Debugging is part of R

You will see:

- messages,
- warnings,
- errors.

That is normal.

The goal is not to avoid every error.

The goal is to learn how to understand and fix them.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Messages, warnings, errors

### Message

R is telling you something.

### Warning

R completed the operation, but something may need attention.

### Error

R stopped because something went wrong.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Read the error

Example:

``` r
plot(grafics)
```

R may say:

``` text
Error: object 'grafics' not found
```

Start with the message.

What is R telling you?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Common things to check

- Did I spell the object correctly?
- Did I run the line that creates the object?
- Is the object in the Environment?
- Did I load the package?
- Are parentheses and commas correct?
- Is the file path correct?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Inspect the object

When code fails, check the object.

``` r
class(recordTable)

str(recordTable)

head(recordTable)

names(recordTable)

dim(recordTable)
```

Do not only inspect the code.

Inspect the data being used by the code.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Search for the error

Most errors have happened to someone else before.

Useful search:

``` text
R ggplot2 object not found
```

Less useful search:

``` text
object not found
```

Include:

``` text
R
package name
function name
important part of the error
```

![](https://gpandradep.github.io/R-CameraTrap-Workshop//images/module-06/frygoogle.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Ask better questions

Not very useful:

``` text
My code does not work.
```

Much more useful:

``` text
I am trying to make a bar plot of Species.

This is my code:

ggplot(recordTable, aes(x = Species))
  geom_bar()

This is the error:

Error: unexpected symbol

What should I check?
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Using AI tools

AI tools can help you:

- interpret errors,
- explain code,
- suggest things to check,
- identify syntax problems,
- explain arguments.

But use them as a learning tool.

Not as something that does your thinking for you.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## AI can be wrong

::::: columns
::: {.column width="35%"}
Always:

1.  Read the suggested code.
2.  Run it yourself.
3.  Inspect the result.
4.  Ask whether the result makes sense.
5.  Check documentation when needed.
:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
![](https://gpandradep.github.io/R-CameraTrap-Workshop//images/module-06/homer.webp){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::::

::: callout-important
Do not copy and run code that you do not understand.
:::
